abstract: A Goldman Sachs Exchanges episode, recorded June 2026 and published 2026-07-02, in which Allison Nathan interviews three people who rarely appear in the same place: Joseph Briggs, who leads Goldman's global economics team and owns the firm's 9%/15M displacement forecast, and MIT's Daron Acemoglu and Neil Thompson. Its value to jobsdata.ai is that it puts a hard number on Acemoglu's ceiling. Asked how big AI's labor-market impact will be, he says he expects net job losses within five years but 'nothing anywhere close to the kinds of things that some expect. I would say less than two to four percent.' That is a directly plottable share-of-US-jobs estimate from the most-cited skeptic in the field, and it sits far below the OpenAI (18%), WEF (8%) and Goldman (9%) projections already on the chart. The episode also surfaces Acemoglu's explanation for the ceiling — a missing application layer, not a capability limit — and Briggs's current-imprint estimate of a 10-15K/month drag on payrolls.
keyFindings: Acemoglu's headline number: 'I would expect some net job losses, limited, but net job losses within the next five years... none of this, in my estimation, will be of a scale anywhere close to the kinds of things that some expect. I would say less than two to four percent.'

His mechanism for the ceiling is deployment, not capability: 'we don't have easy to use applications based on the foundation models that can be adopted by many large-scale employers... we would really need to rely on these applications and we're not seeing those applications yet.' He wants 'the Microsoft Office version of AI.'

Coding is the stated exception, for two compounding reasons: 'the models are already quite capable in coding because parts of coding have now been quite routinized' and 'the people in the software engineering space are all quite experts in AI, so they can give the right prompts and then troubleshoot and check the work.'

Size of the vulnerable pool: cognitive routine work — 'tasks like customer service reps or back-office work' — totals 'eight million in the United States, nine million. So that's not a small amount but also not huge.'

Longer horizon is worse and investment-contingent: 'I would expect bigger net job losses within the next 10 to 15 years if things continue like this,' because complementary AI 'is actually quite productive. It's just that we haven't invested in it.'

The wildcard: 'The big, big, big wildcard, is the integration of AI and robotics... if there were amazing breakthroughs there, that would open up the number of jobs that AI would impact hugely. Physical tasks is about 50% of the work in the US economy.' He orders the next exposure layers as judgment/middle-management work, then socially interactive work.

Briggs on the current imprint: combining tech, management consulting and graphic design, 'there's probably a 10 to 15,000 drag on month-over-month job growth from AI impacts. All that being said, it's still a fairly narrow labor market shock, and we're not seeing a big impact today on the broader economy.'

Briggs restates Goldman's forecast chain: a 15% productivity uplift after full adoption, combined with the historical productivity-to-displacement elasticity, implies 'around nine percent of all workers in the US will be reallocated to new positions during the AI transition' — 15 million workers over 10 years — but 'the unemployment rate increase in any given year would be less than one percentage point.'

Briggs's reabsorption case: 'over the last 80 years, around 85% of job growth has been driven by the technological creation of new positions,' and 'even a five percent acceleration in the pace at which new jobs are being created would be more than enough to reabsorb the workers that we're expecting will be displaced.'

Thompson's framing: his research finds AI arrives as a 'rising tide' rather than a 'crashing wave' — anticipable and manageable rather than sudden — and he cautions that partial automation of a job need not shrink it, though 'if 30% of my job got automated, that might decrease the demand for my job by 30%.'
methodology: Edited podcast transcript, not a paper. Nathan interviewed Acemoglu and Thompson separately and Briggs in a third segment, then intercut them; there is no direct exchange between the economists. No original data collection. Briggs's figures are restatements of published Goldman Sachs Research estimates (the 15% productivity uplift, the 9%/15M ten-year reallocation forecast, the sector-based monthly payroll drag). Acemoglu's 2-4% is an informal verbal estimate given in conversation, not derived on air and not tied to a cited model run, though it is consistent in direction with his published task-based macro work. Thompson references 'one of our recent papers' on crashing waves versus rising tides without naming it.
qualifiers: Tier 2. The central caution is that Acemoglu's 2-4% is a spoken upper bound — the exact phrasing is 'less than two to four percent' — over a five-year horizon, whereas the chart it enters is framed to 2030. It is plotted as a midpoint of 3 with a 2-4 band, which is the honest reading of a range but slightly overstates it relative to the 'less than' hedge; treat it as a soft ceiling rather than a central estimate. It is also an off-the-cuff interview number with no published derivation, so it should not be weighted as if it were a modeled result, and it is a net figure (losses after offsetting creation) while several projections on the same chart are gross. Briggs's 10-15K/month is a narrower sectoral cut than the 16K/month figure already ingested from the Elsie Peng substitution-augmentation work, so the two are close but not the same construct and should not be treated as a revision of one another. Goldman is a sell-side firm with a commercial stake in AI capex, though on this episode Briggs is the more conservative voice. Acemoglu's physical-tasks-are-50%-of-work figure sizes an exposed pool, not an automated share, so it cannot be plotted against the robots chart.
